title: Sahih al-Bukhari
hook: a book that opens with intention, built from reports al-Bukhari judged sound

segments.voice: Yesterday, exposing the fabrications, and your line: they checked. Did you pause before passing something on? Day one thousand one hundred fifty-two.

Actions are judged by intentions, and each person gets what they intended. We traced those words through their chain a week ago. Now look at where they sit. Open Sahih al-Bukhari to its first page, and that's where it begins: a report from Umar ibn al-Khattab that the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said those words. Before a single ruling about prayer, or fasting, or buying and selling, the reader meets a quiet question. Why are you here, opening this book? Since tracing that chain, we've watched scholars weigh narrators, travel for single reports and expose the fakes. All that checking had to end up somewhere. One of the places it ended up is today's word. Sahih al-Bukhari.
screen: `ACTIONS ARE JUDGED BY INTENTIONS.` → `THE FIRST PAGE.` → `WHERE ALL THE CHECKING LED.`

segments.voice: First, the name. Sahih means sound, healthy, whole: the grade we met a few days ago, the top of the scale. Al-Bukhari is the man, Muhammad ibn Isma'il, called after Bukhara, the city he came from. People often just call his book the Sahih, the sound one. Second, the sifting. Tradition says al-Bukhari heard a vast number of reports on his travels and kept only a small share of them: the ones whose chains passed his test, each narrator trustworthy and careful, each one known to have heard from the person before him. Tradition also says that before writing each hadith into the book, he washed and prayed. Whether every detail of that story is exact or not, it shows what the book meant to the people who told it. Third, the headings. Al-Bukhari set the reports under chapter titles he wrote himself, and those titles are often small arguments. A heading states a point, and the hadith beneath it back the point up. Scholars have a saying that al-Bukhari's understanding is in his headings. So the book isn't only a store of reports. It's also one careful reader's reading of them. Fourth, the place it holds. In Sunni scholarship, this book holds a special trust, and with tomorrow's book it makes up the pair called the two Sahihs. Some communities gather to read it aloud, cover to cover, and celebrate when they finish. Shia Muslims have their own collections and their own science of grading, which this path reaches in a few days. And remember where it starts. Before the rulings, the question of intention.
screen: `SAHIH: SOUND, HEALTHY, WHOLE.` · `A SMALL SHARE, CAREFULLY KEPT.` · `HIS UNDERSTANDING IS IN HIS HEADINGS.` · `READ ALOUD, COVER TO COVER.`

segments.voice: The practice: read one hadith from Bukhari. Here's one from its book of good manners, in plain words. Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day should say something good, or keep quiet. Settle, and breathe. Say it to yourself once, slowly. Then think about the conversations ahead of you today: at work, at home, in a group chat that's already buzzing. Where would the second half of that sentence help? Keep quiet. Hold that one place in mind. If you'd like, later today, find that hadith in a translation of the Sahih and read the whole report. The bell holds the time.
Sahih al-Bukhari. The sound collection: the reports al-Bukhari judged firm enough to keep, set under headings he wrote himself. Today's word.

Your line: the sound collection. Today, before you say something about someone, run it through that hadith: something good, or nothing at all. Tomorrow: Sahih Muslim. Day one thousand one hundred fifty-two.

howItsDone: Sunni Muslims study Sahih al-Bukhari with teachers, cite its hadith by number, and in some communities gather to read it aloud from beginning to end.

notes: Claims rule: the outline's 'most trusted Sunni collection' and 'over 600,000 reports' are deliberately not stated; replaced with 'a special trust' and 'tradition says ... a vast number ... a small share'. Confirm the softened framing.
Bukhari 1 (actions are by intentions, narrated by Umar ibn al-Khattab) as the first hadith: confirm.
Bukhari 6018 (speak good or keep silent) in Kitab al-Adab: confirm number and book.
Bukhari's condition that each narrator be known to have heard from (met) the one before him: a summary of how scholars describe his conditions; confirm wording.
Tradition that he washed (ghusl/wudu) and prayed two rak'ahs before entering each hadith: framed as tradition; confirm.
Saying 'fiqh al-Bukhari fi tarajimihi' (his understanding is in his chapter headings): confirm it is fairly called a saying of scholars.
Communal readings and completions (khatm) of Bukhari: stated as 'some communities'; confirm.
